extracted.intended_audience: general public; readers/researchers interested in journalism, media ethics, and the Stephen Glass scandal
extracted.subtask_description: A biographical account illustrating standards and failures in journalistic practice—truthfulness, sourcing, fact‑checking, editorial responsibility—and related professional consequences (e.g., bar moral‑fitness). Useful for evaluating journalistic integrity and verification processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / truthfulness in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The magazine determined the majority of stories he wrote were either partially or entirely fabricated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting must not invent events, people, or quotations; fabrications (partial or whole) constitute serious misconduct. Examples: at least 27 of 41 New Republic articles contained fabricated material; 'Hack Heaven' was completely made up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source transparency / identification of sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass's articles often relied on unnamed or partially identified sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overreliance on anonymous or partially identified sources undermines credibility and makes verification difficult. Publications and reporters should prefer verifiable, identified sources where possible and clearly justify anonymity when used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact‑checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Forbes reporter Adam Penenberg fact‑checked 'Hack Heaven' and failed to find corroborating evidence (e.g., no records for 'Jukt Micronics', no tax filings, nonexistent conference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fact‑checking should verify existence of organizations, conferences, and factual claims using public records, tax filings, registries, and direct confirmation. Lack of such verification may expose fabrications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate quotations and incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Some pieces contained real reporting interwoven with fabricated quotations and incidents; others contained fabricated quotations in profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations and recounted incidents must be accurate and attributable. Fabricating quotes or incidents is a clear ethical breach; publications should correct and retract when discovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of deceptive practices designed to thwart verification
rubrics_metrics.description: In creating 'Hack Heaven', Glass created a website and voicemail account for Jukt Micronics; fabricated notes; printed fake business cards; composed fake community newsletters to avoid detection by fact checkers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any deliberate efforts to manufacture corroborating evidence (fake websites, phone numbers, documents, or personas) are fraudulent and justify termination and retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial oversight and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Republic initially defended Glass though later investigations revealed widespread fabrication; editors and owners bear responsibility for vetting reporters and responding to credible challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must exercise appropriate oversight, respond promptly to credible allegations, and review prior work when significant concerns arise. Defensiveness or delay can exacerbate institutional harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction, retraction, and removal of unreliable content
rubrics_metrics.description: Harper's retracted a story after Glass admitted fabrication; This American Life removed segments 'because of questions about [their] truthfulness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publications should correct the record, issue retractions where warranted, and remove or clearly flag content deemed unreliable. Transparent statements to readers are part of ethical remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability via restitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass sent Harper's Magazine a check for $10,000 and has stated he repaid $200,000 to various publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repayment of ill‑gotten earnings and other forms of restitution may be part of accountability, though they do not erase reputational or professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability limits of anonymous sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: Rolling Stone and Harper's found material 'generally accurate' but said they had no way of verifying information because Glass had cited anonymous sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When anonymous sources are used, editors should seek independent corroboration; otherwise, the material's verifiability is limited and the publication should disclose the limits to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral character / fitness for professional licensure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Committee of Bar Examiners refused to certify Glass on its moral‑fitness test, citing ethics concerns related to his journalistic malpractice; the California Supreme Court ultimately denied admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A pattern of deliberate deception and dishonesty in prior professional conduct can disqualify applicants from licensure that requires demonstration of good moral character. Professional bodies evaluate honesty, remediation, and continued trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and full disclosure in proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The court found 'instances of dishonesty and disingenuousness persisting' and was troubled by 'hypocrisy and evasiveness' in Glass's testimony; it noted he did not admit the full extent of his fabrications until bar proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincere, complete admission of past wrongdoing and candor during investigations or licensure proceedings are critical; evasiveness or delayed admissions weigh heavily against claims of rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of contrition and rehabilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates around Glass's public contrition—some described it as 'careerism of his repentance'—and panels on journalistic ethics questioned whether his remorse was genuine or instrumental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of reform should be assessed for consistency over time, concrete reparative actions (e.g., restitution, corrections), and demonstrable behavioral change. Superficial or performative apologies may not satisfy professional or public expectations.
